lead: An invertible linear map is a linear map that another linear map can undo. It pairs each output with exactly one input. This lets us translate problems between two vector spaces without losing information. It appears in coordinate changes, computer graphics, and solving equations. Only a few universities teach this chapter. In finite dimensions, the practical test is simple: the matrix must be square and its determinant nonzero.
prereq: You need: linear maps, kernel and range, rank-nullity, matrices of linear maps, and Unit 1 on invertible matrices and determinants (see Unit 1, Matrices and Systems of Linear Equations).

blocks.text: Let V and W be vector spaces over the same field F. A linear map T: V → W is invertible if there is a map T⁻¹: W → V such that T⁻¹T = I_V and TT⁻¹ = I_W. Here I_V(v)=v for every v in V, and I_W(w)=w for every w in W. The inverse is unique. Equivalently, T is invertible exactly when T is bijective: one-to-one and onto. Some syllabi call this a non-singular linear transformation.
T⁻¹(T(v)) = v for all v ∈ V, and T(T⁻¹(w)) = w for all w ∈ W.
blocks.where: v is any input in V; w is any input in W; I_V and I_W are identity maps.

blocks.text: The inverse T⁻¹ is itself linear. Take w₁, w₂ ∈ W and a ∈ F. Let v₁=T⁻¹(w₁) and v₂=T⁻¹(w₂). Then T(v₁+v₂)=w₁+w₂, so T⁻¹(w₁+w₂)=v₁+v₂=T⁻¹(w₁)+T⁻¹(w₂). Also T(a v₁)=a w₁, so T⁻¹(a w₁)=a v₁=aT⁻¹(w₁). Linearity of T⁻¹ follows.

For finite-dimensional V and W, T: V → W is invertible if and only if dim V = dim W and ker T = {0}. The kernel is the set of inputs mapped to zero, covered in kernel and range. If dim V = dim W and ker T = {0}, then rank-nullity gives rank T = dim V = dim W. The range is a subspace of W with the same dimension, so range T = W; T is onto. Kernel zero makes T one-to-one. Conversely, invertible T has both properties.

Choose bases. The matrix A of T is square only when dim V = dim W. Then T is invertible exactly when det A ≠ 0. This determinant test needs a square matrix. When T is invertible, the matrix of T⁻¹ is A⁻¹. An isomorphism is an invertible linear map. Two spaces are isomorphic, written V ≅ W, when such a map exists. Finite-dimensional spaces over the same field are isomorphic exactly when their dimensions are equal. Over R, every n-dimensional space is isomorphic to Rⁿ.

figure.caption: T is a bijection from V to W; T⁻¹ sends each w back to the unique v with T(v)=w.

spec.title: Inverse map
spec.aria: A loop diagram shows T taking V to W bijectively and T inverse taking W back to V.

examples.question: Let T: R² → R² be T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − 3y). Show T is invertible. Find T⁻¹(1, 0).
steps: Write the matrix in the standard basis: A = [[2, 1], [1, −3]].
det A = −7 ≠ 0, so A is invertible and T is invertible.
Solve A [x; y] = [1; 0]: 2x + y = 1 and x − 3y = 0.
From x = 3y, substitute: 6y + y = 1, so 7y = 1 and y = 1/7.
examples.answer: T is invertible because det A = −7 ≠ 0, and T⁻¹(1, 0) = (3/7, 1/7).
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
A = [[2, 1], [1, -3]]
b = [1, 0]
det = A[0][0]*A[1][1] - A[0][1]*A[1][0]
x = Fraction(b[0]*A[1][1] - A[0][1]*b[1], det)
y = Fraction(A[0][0]*b[1] - b[0]*A[1][0], det)
print(det)
print(float(x))
print(float(y))

traps: A linear map can be one-to-one without being onto when dim V ≠ dim W. Check dimensions before calling it invertible.
A square matrix with determinant 0 is not invertible. It may still map some nonzero vector to zero.
Do not call T invertible just because one equation T(v)=w has a solution. Every w in W must have exactly one solution.
The determinant test applies only to square matrices. A 2×3 matrix has no determinant and cannot represent an invertible map between R³ and R².

quiz.a: A linear map T: V → W with T⁻¹: W → V satisfying T⁻¹T = I_V and TT⁻¹ = I_W.

quiz.q: Why is the inverse of a linear map linear? Give the two preserved operations.
quiz.a: It preserves addition and scalar multiplication: T⁻¹(w₁+w₂)=T⁻¹(w₁)+T⁻¹(w₂) and T⁻¹(a w)=aT⁻¹(w).

quiz.q: State the finite-dimensional criterion for T: V → W to be invertible.
quiz.a: T is invertible exactly when dim V = dim W and ker T = {0}; equivalently, its matrix is square with nonzero determinant.

quiz.q: T: R² → R² is T(x, y) = (3x, y). Find T⁻¹(6, 5).
A 3×3 matrix A represents T. If det A = 0, is T invertible? Why?
quiz.a: No. A square matrix with determinant 0 is not invertible, so T is not invertible.

quiz.q: V has dimension 3, W has dimension 2. Can a linear map T: V → W be invertible? Explain.
quiz.a: No. An invertible map needs dim V = dim W. Rank-nullity also forces nullity at least 1, so T is not one-to-one.

beyond: Not for the exam. In functional analysis, invertible bounded operators and the inverse mapping theorem extend these ideas to infinite dimensions. In computer vision, camera calibration uses invertible linear maps to switch coordinate frames. In machine learning, invertible linear layers appear in normalizing flows. Search for "linear isomorphism", "inverse mapping theorem", and "change of basis matrix inverse".
